I farm in Quzhou County, so at the start of the season I would keep to the cropping pattern I trust most on the North China Plain: winter wheat followed by summer maize. At my age, with my education and the way I make decisions, I would not chase complicated cash crops this year. Grain is easier for me to manage, I know the field work well, and the machinery, irrigation timing, fertilizer use, and pest control are all familiar. That matters to me because I want steady output and lower risk more than I want to gamble on a higher-price crop I do not know as well.

I would put all my land into the wheat-maize rotation. For the wheat that is already in the ground from the previous autumn, I would manage it carefully through spring with one topdressing of nitrogen, irrigation at key stages, and disease and aphid control only when pressure shows up. After harvest, I would move quickly into summer maize, because getting it sown on time is important for yield here. For maize, I would use hybrid seed, give enough fertilizer for strong early growth, irrigate when the rains are not enough, and keep weeds and insects under control with a few well-timed sprays. For tillage, I would mostly use rotary tillage because it fits my labor, machinery, and the wheat-maize double-cropping schedule. My goal is stable grain yield, manageable costs, and work I can carry through without making the season too risky.
